etymology: From Greek Ptolemaïs, the Hellenistic name of Accho on the Phoenician coast; a harbor city Paul visited on his return toward Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Ptolemais is the coastal city where Paul and his company landed after sailing from Tyre, saluted the brethren, and abode one day before going on to Caesarea (Acts 21:7). In the Old Testament the site is Accho, allotted to Asher yet long held by the nations. By the New Testament the harbor bears a Greek royal name, a reminder that empires rename coasts while the church still finds saints there. The narrative is spare: landing, greeting, one night’s fellowship, then the road toward Jerusalem and bonds. Ptolemais is not a stage for miracles in the text. It is a way-station of ordinary communion under providence. The modern reader is tempted to skip such places as filler between greater scenes. Luke will not. He tracks the ship, the harbor, and the brethren so that the church sees Christ building his people along real coasts under real kings. Ptolemais stands as a Phoenician door between sea and Judea, where the gospel traveler finds a day of rest among the faithful before the harder road inland. Remember the place, and remember that the Lord staffs even brief harbors with saints who can be saluted by name in a single day.

etymology: From Greek Mitulēnē, chief city of Lesbos; a port of call on Paul’s return voyage through the Aegean (Acts 20:14).
biblical_def: Mitylene is the Lesbos harbor where Paul’s company arrived after meeting at Assos, as Luke tracks the coastal return toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:13–14). The note is brief, yet it anchors the gospel in Aegean geography: real islands, real overnight sails, real sequencing of ports. Paul had chosen to walk to Assos while the ship rounded the cape; at Mitylene the company is together again under the same Lord who rules wind and timetable. The detail resists every effort to dissolve Acts into myth. Christ’s apostle moves under ordinary winds and harbors, and the Spirit still records the names. Mitylene is not the scene of a sermon in the text. It is a night’s landing on the road of obedience. The church that loves Scripture will love such names, for they prove that redemption walked streets and slept in ports. When modern piety prefers abstract journey language to maps, Mitylene answers: the Lord of glory used Lesbos as a stepping-stone toward Jerusalem and the bonds that would carry the gospel to Rome. Hold the harbor, and you hold a faith that is not ashamed of history’s small places.

etymology: From Greek Chios, an island of the eastern Aegean; Luke notes the ship came ‘over against Chios’ on the day after Mitylene (Acts 20:15).
biblical_def: Chios is the Aegean island past which Paul’s ship sailed the day after Mitylene, on the measured run toward Samos and Miletus (Acts 20:15). Luke does not invent romance; he logs bearings. ‘Over against Chios’ is a sailor’s phrase fixed in holy writ. The apostle is hasting toward Jerusalem for Pentecost, and the Spirit still records intermediate islands so that no day of obedience is lost to fog. Chios therefore teaches the church to honor the particularity of providence. God does not save a vague world; He moves His servants past named shores under named calendars. The island itself receives no sermon in the text, yet its name is a stake in the ground against mythic reading. When higher criticism dissolves Acts into theological fiction, Chios answers from the chart: this is a voyage that can be followed. The believer who loves the Lord will not despise small place-names. They are the footsteps of obedience between greater cities, and they bind the gospel to the same creation maps men still sail under the same Creator who numbered all the isles.

etymology: From Greek Samos, an island near the coast of Asia Minor; Paul’s company arrived there the day after Chios and tarried at Trogyllium before Miletus (Acts 20:15).
biblical_def: Samos is the island station between Chios and Miletus on Paul’s measured return through the Aegean (Acts 20:15). Luke pairs Samos with Trogyllium, a coastal stop, showing a ship working the shore-route with overnight precision. The apostle is not wandering. He is hasting to Jerusalem, yet every harbor is written down. Samos thus stands for the discipline of providence in mission: haste without erasing place. The modern church often wants either pure efficiency or pure mysticism. Acts gives neither. It gives days, islands, and elders waiting at Miletus. Samos is the quiet middle of that chain. No miracle is attached in the verse, and that is the point. The Lord’s work includes ordinary landings on the way to tearful farewells and holy warnings. When the reader races to Miletus for the speech, he must still pass Samos. Geography is not an obstacle to doctrine; it is the floor on which doctrine walked. Hold Samos, and you hold a faith that can be plotted on a map without shame before a watching world that still sails those same waters under the same Lord.

etymology: KJV form of Cos (Greek Kōs), an island of the Dodecanese; Paul’s company came to Coos with a straight course after the Miletus farewell (Acts 21:1).
biblical_def: Coos is the island reached with a straight course after Paul tore himself from the Ephesian elders at Miletus (Acts 21:1). The verse is a hinge: tears behind, Jerusalem bonds ahead, and between them a clean sail to Coos, then Rhodes, then Patara. The KJV retains the older English form Coos; the place is the well-known island of Cos. Luke’s ‘straight course’ is not poetry first; it is seamanship under providence. The gospel does not float in allegory. It runs a measured track across the Aegean after a shepherd’s farewell. Coos therefore belongs to the theology of departure: when the Lord calls a man on, even the first night’s island is written down. The church that forgets Coos will also forget that obedience has waypoints. Do not spiritualize away the map. The same Christ who warned of bonds at Jerusalem first guided the ship to Coos with a straight course, then on through Rhodes and Patara toward Tyre and the brethren who would plead with tears. Geography is pastoral care written in harbors. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Greek Rhodos, the great island and city of the southern Aegean; Paul’s company reached Rhodes the day after Coos (Acts 21:1).
biblical_def: Rhodes is the island and harbor on the day-following after Coos, before Patara, in Paul’s launch from the elders of Ephesus toward Phenicia (Acts 21:1). The name is famous in the ancient world for ships and trade, yet Luke mentions it only as a link in the chain of obedience. That restraint is itself instructive. Scripture does not flatter tourist fame; it tracks the apostle. Rhodes becomes holy not by pagan colossus or commercial renown, but by bearing for a day the men who carried the gospel toward Jerusalem. The church learns here to measure places by the presence of Christ’s servants, not by the world’s monuments. After tears at Miletus, the company runs a clean coastal sequence: Coos, Rhodes, Patara, then a Phenician ship. Rhodes is the middle bead on that string. Ignore it, and you begin to treat Acts as a sermon anthology with scenic backdrops. Keep it, and you keep a voyage that really happened under the Lord who numbers the isles as a little thing and still writes their names when His servants sleep there. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Greek Patara, a Lycian seaport; the harbor where Paul’s company found a ship sailing over unto Phenicia (Acts 21:1–2).
biblical_def: Patara is the Lycian port that closes the island run from Coos and Rhodes and opens the open-sea leg toward Phenicia (Acts 21:1–2). Here the travelers change ships: finding a vessel sailing over unto Phenicia, they went aboard and set forth. The detail is logistical and theological at once. Providence is not only miracles; it is also a berth available when the Lord wills the next stage. Patara therefore stands as a hinge harbor between the Aegean chain and the Syrian coast. From this quay the company will sight Cyprus on the left hand and land at Tyre. Luke’s care with the transfer rebukes every reading that treats travel notes as unspiritual. The gospel advances by ordinary means under extraordinary purpose. A ship is found; a course is set; brethren will soon be saluted at Tyre and Ptolemais. Patara is the uncelebrated door of that advance. The church that prays for open doors should notice how often Scripture’s open doors look like harbors, schedules, and faithful companions rather than fireworks. Hold Patara, and hold a sober doctrine of means. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: KJV form for Phoenix (Greek Phoinix), a harbor of Crete looking toward the southwest and northwest; desired as a wintering port in Paul’s voyage to Rome (Acts 27:12).
biblical_def: Phenice is the Cretan harbor the majority advised to reach when Fair Havens was judged incommodious to winter in (Acts 27:12). The haven of Phenice is described as lying toward the southwest and northwest, a double exposure sailors could evaluate. Paul had already warned of hurt and much damage; the centurion believed the master and owner of the ship more than the apostle. The soft south wind then tempted them past the warning, and the Euroclydon took the vessel. Phenice therefore is not only a place-name. It is the chosen alternative that never became the safe winter of their plans. The text teaches the difference between technical seamanship and prophetic warning, and the cost of majority counsel against the word of God’s servant. Modern readers often moralize the storm without the map. Luke keeps both. Fair Havens, Phenice, Clauda, and Malta are the stations of a providence that still judges pride in professional confidence. Recover Phenice as the harbor they wanted and did not keep, and you recover a sober fear of ignoring clear warning under fair weather. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew ʾĀbēl Miṣrayim, “meadow (or mourning) of Egypt”; the name the Canaanites gave the threshingfloor of Atad where Joseph mourned Jacob (Gen 50:11).
biblical_def: Abel-mizraim is the name fixed upon the threshingfloor of Atad beyond Jordan when Joseph and the Egyptians mourned Jacob with a great and very sore lamentation (Gen 50:10–11). The inhabitants of the land said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians; therefore the name Abel-mizraim. The place is geography and testimony. Egypt’s grief for Israel’s patriarch is written on Canaanite soil, and the burial train of Jacob becomes a public witness before the nations. Joseph keeps his oath to bury his father in the cave of the field of Machpelah, yet the mourning is so great that the land itself receives a new name. Abel-mizraim therefore stands against every attempt to privatize grief or to empty patriarchal history into myth. A real father dies; a real son weeps; a real floor of grain becomes a floor of lament; a real name is coined by onlookers. The church reads it as providence honoring the patriarchs and as a foreshadow of greater mourning and greater hope. Hold the name, and hold the public seriousness of death under the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

biblical_def: Atad is the threshingfloor beyond Jordan that becomes the stage of Jacob’s seven-day mourning before the burial in Machpelah (Gen 50:10–11). The floor is a place of grain and labor; Scripture turns it into a place of grievous lamentation. Joseph, the sons of Israel, and the Egyptian escort stop there with a great and very sore lamentation. The Canaanites watch and name the site Abel-mizraim. Atad therefore teaches that holy history claims ordinary workplaces. A threshingfloor is not too low for covenant grief. The modern world privatizes death and sterilizes public lament; Genesis shows a train of mourners large enough to rename the land. Atad also stands ‘beyond Jordan,’ fixing the approach to Canaan for the burial of the patriarch who had made Joseph swear. The geography of oath-keeping is not vague. The church that honors the fathers will not skip Atad as a minor stop. It is the floor where Egypt wept for Israel’s prince, and where providence wrote mourning into the map before the cave of Machpelah received the body. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew ʾĀbēl hashshiṭṭīm, “meadow of the acacias”; the plains camp of Israel in Moab before Jordan (Num 33:49).
biblical_def: Abel-shittim is the final meadow-camp of Israel in the plains of Moab by Jordan near Jericho, listed among the stations of the wilderness journey (Num 33:49). It is the acacia-meadow at the edge of promise, where the nation encamped before the crossing. Nearby Shittim is also the scene of the Baal-peor snare (Num 25), so the same region holds both readiness for inheritance and the memory of gross idolatry. Abel-shittim therefore teaches the church that the threshold of blessing is not a safe zone for presumption. God can station His people at the door of the land and still judge sin in the camp. The name ties ordinary flora—acacias used also for tabernacle wood—to a national campsite under Moses and Joshua. Do not romanticize the meadow. It is holy ground of providence and a warning ground of compromise. The modern habit is to speak of ‘arriving’ without repentance. Abel-shittim answers: you may pitch at the edge of promise and still need the zeal of Phinehas and the word of God. Hold the place, and hold both hope and holiness at the Jordan’s brink.

etymology: From Aramaic/Hebrew ʾAḥməṯā, Ecbatana; the palace city in the province of the Medes where Cyrus’s decree was found (Ezra 6:2).

When adversaries stalled the temple work, search was made in Babylon; the decisive document surfaced at Achmetha. The place therefore stands for providence over archives. Empires store paper; God uses their paper to rebuild His house. Achmetha is not Israel’s capital. It is a foreign palace whose records serve Zion. The church learns here that opposition does not cancel written decree, and that the Lord can retrieve a forgotten roll at the hour it is needed. Modern unbelief treats Ezra’s document trail as pious invention. The text answers with place, province, and royal memorandum. Recover Achmetha, and recover confidence that history’s filing rooms are under the same God who stirs kings’ spirits. The temple rose not by vibes but by decree found, confirmed, and enforced from a Median palace to Jerusalem’s rubble. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew ʾĂdummīm, “red places”; the ascent of Adummim on the border between Judah and Benjamin, on the Jericho road (Jos 15:7; 18:17).
biblical_def: Adummim is the ascent named in the border descriptions of Judah and Benjamin, on the wilderness road that climbs from the Jordan rift toward Jerusalem (Jos 15:7; 18:17). The name means red places, fitting the ruddy rock of that pass. Scripture fixes it as a boundary marker, not a tourist legend. The road later associated with the parable of the wounded traveler runs through this wild ascent between Jerusalem and Jericho. Adummim therefore stands for border truth and road danger under the same Lord who allotting tribes. Modern readers often know the parable and forget the map. Joshua wrote Adummim into the cadastral holy land before any New Testament illustration. Recover the ascent as covenant geography: God draws lines, names passes, and assigns inheritances in real terrain. The church that despises border chapters will also despise providence in ordinary jurisdiction. Hold Adummim, and you hold a red climb on the way of tribal lots—and a sober reminder that the road between sacred city and low plain has always been a place where neighbors prove or fail their love under God’s eye.

etymology: From Hebrew ʾAhăwā, a river (or canal) district where Ezra proclaimed a fast before the return caravan entered the dangerous road (Ezr 8:15, 21, 31).
biblical_def: Ahava is the river-camp where Ezra assembled returning exiles, found no Levites at first, then proclaimed a fast that they might afflict themselves before God to seek of Him a right way for themselves, their little ones, and their substance (Ezr 8:15, 21). Ezra was ashamed to ask a band of soldiers of the king, because he had told the king that the hand of God is upon all them for good that seek Him. At Ahava they fasted and besought God, and He was intreated of them; later they departed from the river of Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month (Ezr 8:31). Ahava is therefore the school of dependent courage. Faith does not deny danger; it refuses to make unbelief’s request after a public confession of God’s hand. The modern church often wants either armed presumption or prayerless planning. Ezra gives fasting, little ones, substance, and a road under the hand of God. Hold Ahava, and hold the doctrine that seeking the Lord is the first logistics of any holy journey home to Zion under hostile powers.

etymology: From Hebrew ʾAshtərōth Qarnayim, “Ashtaroth of the two horns”; a city of the Rephaim smitten by Chedorlaomer in Genesis 14:5.
biblical_def: Ashteroth Karnaim is the two-horned Ashtaroth where Chedorlaomer and the kings with him smote the Rephaim in the days of Abraham (Gen 14:5). The name binds a place to the goddess Ashtoreth and to horned might, yet the narrative is not pagan triumph. It is the ledger of a war that will soon touch Lot and draw Abram into battle and blessing under Melchizedek. Ashteroth Karnaim therefore stands at the edge of the first great international conflict in Scripture’s patriarchal history. Giants fall to eastern kings; then the friend of God pursues and recovers. The modern reader is tempted either to mythologize the Rephaim or to baptize Near Eastern goddess-cult as ‘ancient spirituality.’ Genesis does neither. It names the city, records the stroke, and moves on to Abram’s faith and Melchizedek’s bread and wine. Hold Ashteroth Karnaim as real geography under real war, and hold the God who later forbids Israel the worship of Ashtaroth while still writing her place-names into the true history of the earth He owns. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew Kərīth, a brook before Jordan; the hiding place where Elijah was fed by ravens at the word of the LORD (1Ki 17:3–5).
biblical_def: Cherith is the brook eastward of Jordan where the LORD sent Elijah to hide after he had declared the drought to Ahab (1Ki 17:1–5). There he was to drink of the brook, and the ravens were commanded to feed him bread and flesh morning and evening. Cherith is therefore the school of secret providence. The prophet who confronts kings must first learn to be hidden and supplied by God’s strange means. When the brook dries because there is no rain, the same word moves him to Zarephath. Cherith teaches that obedience has seasons of obscurity that are not abandonment. Modern ministry culture idolizes platform and visibility. Elijah’s first post-oracle assignment is a ravine and birds. Recover Cherith, and recover the doctrine that God’s servants may be buried in a brook-bed while still on the main line of His purpose. The water fails on schedule under the drought Elijah announced; providence is consistent with the prophet’s own word. Hold the brook, and hold a faith that can be fed in secret until the next command. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew Kəbār, a river (canal) of the land of the Chaldeans; the site of Ezekiel’s visions among the captives (Eze 1:1, 3).

The hand of the LORD was there upon him. Chebar is not Zion; it is foreign water under Babylon. Yet the heavens open there. The place teaches that judgment’s geography does not cancel revelation. God is not locked inside the fallen temple’s rubble. He appears to a priest in captivity and commissions him. Modern sentiment either despairs in exile or invents a spirituality that needs no holy place and no holy judgment. Ezekiel at Chebar rebukes both. The captives are truly displaced; the glory is truly present; the word is truly hard. Hold Chebar, and hold a doctrine of God who judges His house and still speaks by rivers of the Chaldeans. The church in any Babylon must not demand Jerusalem’s comforts before she will hear. The wheel and the throne can meet a man on a canal bank when the Lord wills. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew Kasdīm (Chaldeans/Chaldea); the land and people of southern Mesopotamia, associated with Babylon, Ur, and the instrument of Judah’s exile.
biblical_def: Chaldea is the land of the Chaldeans, the Mesopotamian power-sphere tied to Ur of the Chaldees, to Babylon’s rise, and to the rod of the LORD’s anger against Judah. Abram was called out of Ur of the Chaldees; centuries later the Chaldeans come up against Jerusalem as the appointed instrument of judgment. Chaldea is therefore both origin and scourge in redemptive history: the old country left by faith, and the empire that empties Zion under wrath. The prophets do not flatter Chaldea. They name her pride, her idols, and her appointed hour, and they also promise her fall when the cup is finished. Modern discourse often reduces Chaldea to museum archaeology or astrology branding. Scripture presents a moral empire under God. Hold Chaldea, and hold the double lesson of election and judgment: God calls a man out of the Chaldees, and God later raises the Chaldeans to chasten His people, then breaks the rod. Geography is theology when the LORD writes both call and captivity across the same name. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew ʾArgōb, a region of Bashan with threescore cities; taken under Og and allotted in the conquest east of Jordan (Deut 3:4, 13–14).
biblical_def: Argob is the region of Bashan containing threescore cities with walls and bars, taken from Og and remembered as a hard cluster of strongholds (Deut 3:4–5, 13–14). Jair took the region and called the towns Havoth-jair. Argob stands for fortified geography conquered by the gift of God, not by Israel’s native might. The text stresses the cities’ strength so that the conquest will be read as the LORD’s act. Modern unbelief either denies the conquest or moralizes it as raw imperialism without theophany. Deuteronomy answers with command, gift, and named regions. Argob is not a metaphor for inner obstacles first; it is basalt towns in Bashan under Og the giant king. Then, and only then, may the church learn courage for later strongholds. Hold Argob, and hold a faith that names real walls God can give into the hand of His people according to promise—and that refuses to baptize uncommanded violence with holy language. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Akkadian name form preserved in Hebrew Bēlshaʾaṣṣar; the Chaldean king who saw the handwriting on the wall and was slain the same night (Dan 5).
biblical_def: Belshazzar is the king who made a great feast for a thousand of his lords, drank wine from the vessels of the house of God, and praised the gods of gold and silver while the LORD wrote upon the plaster of the wall (Dan 5). Daniel interpreted the writing: God had numbered the kingdom, weighed the king, and divided the realm. That night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was slain. The figure is a warning against sacrilegious pride under judgment already due. He knew of Nebuchadnezzar’s humbling yet lifted himself up. Belshazzar therefore stands for light refused. Modern culture turns the handwriting into a proverb and empties the feast of theology. Scripture keeps vessels, gods, knees smiting, and a kingdom ending at midnight. Hold Belshazzar, and hold the fear of the Lord in public power: sacred things are not party props, and delayed judgment is not canceled judgment. The Most High still numbers, weighs, and divides. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Old Persian royal name via Hebrew/Aramaic ʾArtaxšastā; Persian king(s) in Ezra–Nehemiah who authorized temple and wall work under God’s hand.
biblical_def: Artaxerxes is the Persian throne-name borne in Ezra and Nehemiah by the king who stopped and later advanced the work of God’s house and city according to the turning of providence. Under him letters fly, governors are checked, Nehemiah is cupbearer, and decrees open the road to Jerusalem with timber and protection (Ezr 4; 7; Neh 1–2). Scripture is not naive about empire. Adversaries can cite a king’s name to halt building; the same court can later speed the servant of God. Artaxerxes therefore stands for the LORD’s rule over Gentile crowns for Zion’s sake. The modern church either despises politics as unclean or baptizes princes as messiahs. Ezra–Nehemiah gives a third way: pray, serve, draft letters, and confess that the good hand of God is upon the cupbearer before the king. Hold Artaxerxes as a real monarch under heaven, and hold courage that can ask for letters without trusting the palace more than the God of heaven. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew ʾEbed-melek, “servant of the king”; the Ethiopian eunuch in Zedekiah’s house who drew Jeremiah out of the dungeon (Jer 38–39).
biblical_def: Ebed-melech is the Ethiopian eunuch who heard that Jeremiah had been cast into the dungeon and went to the king to plead for the prophet’s life (Jer 38:7–13). He took men, old cast clouts, and rotten rags, let them down by cords, and drew Jeremiah up. The LORD later promised Ebed-melech deliverance when the city fell, because he had put his trust in Him (Jer 39:15–18). The man is a rebuke to coward princes and a comfort to hidden faith in a collapsing court. Ethnicity and office do not bar courage; the princes of Judah showed less fear of God than this servant. Modern readings either turn him into a mascot for politics or ignore him as a minor cast member. Scripture gives him a personal oracle. Hold Ebed-melech, and hold the doctrine that God sees rags-and-cords mercy under siege, and that trust in the LORD is safer than the city’s walls. The dungeon prophet and the Ethiopian servant meet under providence while kings dither. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Hebrew ʾĂdōnī-ṣedeq, “lord of righteousness”; Amorite king of Jerusalem who led the southern coalition against Gibeon and fell to Joshua (Jos 10).
biblical_def: Adoni-zedek is the king of Jerusalem who heard that Joshua had taken Ai and that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, and who feared greatly (Jos 10:1–5). etymology: From Greek Hananias (Hebrew Hananiah, “Yahweh is gracious”); the high priest who commanded Paul to be struck and whom Paul called a whited wall (Acts 23:2–5).
biblical_def: Ananias the high priest is the ruler who commanded them that stood by Paul to smite him on the mouth when Paul began his defense before the council (Acts 23:1–5). Paul answered, God shall smite thee, thou whited wall; then, being told he reviled the high priest, he cited the law against speaking evil of the ruler of the people. The scene is thick with irony: a man named for the LORD’s grace enforces injustice with a blow, and the apostle both prophesies judgment and submits to the office’s legal dignity. Ananias later appears in the accusation before Felix (Acts 24:1). Hold this Ananias distinct from Ananias of Damascus and from Ananias who lied to the Holy Ghost. The high priest shows how sacred office can be filled by a whitewashed opponent of the gospel. Modern readers either despise all office or excuse all clergy. Paul does neither. He names the hypocrisy and still honors the law of the office. Recover that tension as holy, not as confusion. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Latin Publius; the chief man of the island of Malta who received Paul and was healed in his household (Acts 28:7–8).
biblical_def: Publius is the chief man of Malta who lodged Paul and the shipwrecked company three days courteously after they escaped the sea (Acts 28:7). The father of Publius lay sick of a fever and of a bloody flux; Paul went in, prayed, laid hands on him, and healed him. Others then came and were healed. Publius stands for hospitality under providence after judgment-storm. The islanders first thought Paul a murderer when the viper fastened on his hand; then they changed their minds. In that swirl of pagan interpretation, a chief man opens his estate and receives Christian mercy. Modern missions sometimes despise hospitality as soft work. Acts ties lodging to healing and to the gospel’s advance toward Rome. Hold Publius, and hold courtesy as a means God uses among the nations—not as a substitute for doctrine, but as the open door through which the apostle prays and heals. The chief man’s house becomes a firstfruits station on the road to Caesar. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Greek Philētos, “beloved”; false teacher named with Hymenaeus who erred concerning the truth, saying the resurrection is past already (2Ti 2:17–18).
biblical_def: Philetus is named with Hymenaeus as a man whose word will eat as doth a canker, who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already, and overthrow the faith of some (2Ti 2:17–18). The error is not a small calendar dispute. It empties the future hope of the body and destabilizes believers. Paul sets the correction in the same breath: the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are His. Philetus therefore stands as a warning against sophisticated denials of bodily resurrection hope. Modern theology often repeats his error in new clothes: resurrection as metaphor only, kingdom as already so realized that waiting is naive. Scripture names the canker and commands separation from iniquity. Hold Philetus, and hold pastoral vigilance: names matter, errors spread, and the church must not flatter teachers who overthrow faith while sounding advanced. The beloved name did not make the doctrine safe. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence.

etymology: From Greek Hermogenēs, “born of Hermes”; named with Phygellus among those in Asia who turned away from Paul (2Ti 1:15).
biblical_def: Hermogenes is the companion name to Phygellus in Paul’s lament that all they which are in Asia be turned away from me (2Ti 1:15). His Greek name evokes Hermes, yet the text’s concern is not etymology but desertion. When the apostle became a prisoner, some who had been associated with the Asian work stepped back. Paul writes it to Timothy so that shame of the testimony and of the Lord’s prisoner will not spread as a quiet norm. Hermogenes is a mirror for every generation that loves gospel success and hates gospel chains. The remedy in the chapter is not cynicism but the spirit of power, love, and a sound mind, and the example of Onesiphorus. The Lord’s servant may be left by Asia and still write Scripture under God. etymology: From Greek Nikopolis, “city of victory”; the place where Paul determined to winter and asked Titus to come diligently (Tit 3:12).
biblical_def: Nicopolis is the city where Paul planned to winter when he sent Artemas or Tychicus to Titus and urged Titus to be diligent to come (Tit 3:12). The note is pastoral and practical: gospel work includes seasons, travel, coworkers, and winter quarters. Nicopolis—city of victory—is not a triumph parade in the text. It is a planned base for continued labor. Luke does not narrate this stay in Acts; the Pastoral Epistle supplies the intention. The church learns that apostolic ministry had logistics after the great missionary panels of Acts. Modern romanticism wants only miracles and riots. Paul wants Titus present before winter. Hold Nicopolis, and hold a doctrine of ordered ministry: send reliable men, gather coworkers, plan the cold months under the same Christ who conquered. The name victory belongs first to the Lord; the city is only a wintering place for servants who still have work to do among the churches. The name stands in Scripture so that the church will not invent a thinner story than the one God wrote in places and persons under providence. corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is to treat pastoral logistics as unspiritual. Nicopolis becomes trivia. Paul determines to winter and summons help. Recover ordered means in ministry.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What must be recovered is the plain geography and providence of Scripture: God names places so His people will remember where He acted, judged, and saved. Do not dissolve the map into mood. Hold the place, and hold the LORD who rules it.
